The first thing I learned to mend was the left knee of a pair of green trousers. My mother showed me how to slip a piece of cardboard down the leg so I wouldn’t sew the front to the back. I remember this because I took the cardboard out too soon and sewed the front to the back. For a minute I thought I might still wear them. I was nine. I put my foot in and got as far as the knee.

My mother was on the phone with the gas company. She watched me hop twice, then pointed at the seam ripper without interrupting the account number she was reading aloud.

I’ve kept a piece of cardboard in my sewing tin ever since. The current one is cut from a box of lasagne sheets. Most of what I mend now belongs to my daughter, who wears through her clothes in surprising places. Last winter she brought me a coat with the pocket hanging off on the inside. The outer cloth was untouched. Whatever had happened to it had happened in private.

“What do you keep in here?”

“Just my things.”

I put my hand through the tear. Down in the lining, along the hem, I found three stones, a pound coin, a blue pencil worn to the length of my thumb and a folded note so soft at the creases that it felt like a piece of flannel.

“Do you want this?” I asked.

She snatched it, which answered that. I handed over the pencil and the coin. The stones she said I could throw away.

They were nothing special. Not even good for skimming. I set them on the table, and while I was sewing the pocket she picked one up and rubbed its grey face with a wet finger.

“This one goes purple.”

It did, a little. We watched it dry. Then she wet it again.

My mother used to turn out our pockets into a chipped saucer on top of the washing machine. At the end of the week, anything we hadn’t claimed was hers. This was mostly an incentive to collect our change. But once I found her at the kitchen sink washing a horse chestnut I’d forgotten. It had been in the saucer for months. The shine had gone out of it and the skin was puckered. She polished it with the tea towel and put it in the pocket of her dressing gown.

Years later, when she moved into a flat, we cleared out the house together. I found that dressing gown on a hook behind the bathroom door and reached straight into the pocket. There was a tissue in there, and the little metal key for bleeding the radiators.

“What are you looking for?” she asked.

I told her.

“Oh, love,” she said. “I’ve had about six dressing gowns since that one.”

I don’t know why I’d expected to find the chestnut. I’d thrown away whole sets of furniture in the meantime.

When I finished the coat, my daughter tested the pocket with her fist. She put the pencil back, and the coin, and the folded note. She carried the purple stone upstairs. The other two stayed on the table until supper, when I scooped them up with the crumbs and put them in the bin.

A week later she asked for them.

“I thought you didn’t want them.”

“I didn’t then.”

This struck me as such a reasonable account of being alive that I went outside in my slippers and opened the wheelie bin. Unfortunately it had been emptied that morning. There was nothing at the bottom but a sticker from an apple.

We went looking for replacements. It was nearly dark, and the gravel beside our building was the wrong kind altogether, sharp little chips of yellow. We walked as far as the chemist’s, where a tree had lifted a square of pavement and exposed a pocket of earth. My daughter crouched there and worked a stone loose with her pencil.

“Here,” she said.

I held out my hand. It was brown, flat on one side. I waited while she looked for another, but she had already stood up.

“Is one enough?”

“That one’s yours.”

I almost asked what I was supposed to do with it. Then I put it in my pocket, where there happened to be a hole. We heard it hit the pavement.

My daughter looked at me. I looked at her. She laughed so hard she had to lean against the chemist’s window, and the woman inside, halfway through lowering the blind, stopped to see what was funny.

At home I fetched the lasagne cardboard and my daughter chose some thread. She wanted yellow, though the coat was black. I showed her how to knot the end and how to push the needle away from the hand holding the cloth. Her stitches went in several directions. I had to stop myself from pulling them out and starting again.

When she was done, I tried the stone. It held.

There’s a yellow pucker just below my hip now. From the outside you can see exactly where the pocket ends.
